query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, controlled thermal exposure induces the precipitation of nano-scale, Mg-rich intermetallic phases (especially along grain boundaries) that mediate local changes in diffusion and galvanic coupling. These microstructural changes, in turn, alter the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-cast, homogeneous solid solution state.
generation.material_initial_state: A metastable, primarily homogeneous solid solution containing randomly distributed Mg atoms with minor intermetallic constituents.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging/annealing at moderately high temperatures (e.g., 600–700 °C) under controlled atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled thermal conditions (using a standard dwell time) with subsequent exposure to corrosive media (e.g., salt spray or acidic electrolyte) and high-temperature oxidation tests in air.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates forming preferentially at grain boundaries and/or phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The non-equilibrium processing produces a supersaturated, metastable solid solution. Under thermal activation, local diffusion drives Mg segregation and the nucleation/growth of intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates create micro-galvanic sites and alter diffusion pathways for oxygen, thus changing both the nature and protectiveness of the oxide scales formed at high temperature as well as the dynamics of localized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous state, thermally aged alloys will exhibit a measurable increase in the volume fraction and size of Mg-rich precipitates, accompanied by differences in corrosion metrics (e.g., altered corrosion current density or potential) and a changed high-temperature oxidation behavior characterized by non-uniform oxide scale formation (e.g., altered thickness or composition).
generation.baseline: As-cast, metastable homogeneous Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy without significant precipitation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be observable in alloys designed with density <6 g/cm3 and where the elemental property differences promote intermetallic compound formation, but not in alloys that have already fully transformed to equilibrium phases (i.e., under very long-term aging or excessively high temperatures).
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effects (e.g., the extent of precipitate formation and its direct impact on corrosion/oxidation rates) may vary with exact alloy composition, thermal treatment parameters, and environmental conditions. It is also uncertain whether the micro-galvanic effects of the precipitates will enhance or reduce corrosion resistance overall.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the target Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in their as-cast state. Subject one set to controlled thermal aging (e.g., 600–700 °C for several hours) while maintaining a control set with no aging. Characterize both sets using high-resolution TEM/SEM with EDS to quantify the formation and distribution of Mg-rich precipitates, then perform corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in a standardized electrolyte) and high-temperature oxidation experiments in air with subsequent oxide scale analysis (XRD, SEM-EDS).
measurements: Volume fraction and morphology of precipitates (grain boundary vs. intra-granular) via TEM/SEM
Corrosion current density and potential from electrochemical measurements
Oxide scale thickness, uniformity, and phase composition from XRD and SEM-EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant increase in the volume or distribution of Mg-rich precipitates is observed in the thermally aged samples compared to the as-cast baseline, or if the changes in corrosion behavior and oxidation characteristics (oxide scale thickness/composition) do not differ from the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
